Chan masters use it as a direct answer or final line: apparent progress does not leave an unobstructed road, but meets another pass beyond the last. Baoen Tan gives it as the beneficial lion-roar sentence; Tieguan Fashu answers a claim of face-to-face accord with it; Jingqing Daofu caps the water-moon exchange with it; and Shitian Faxun says it is the answer he would give to that same water-moon question.

Senses.Explanation: A further barrier names an additional gate beyond an earlier passage, commonly in lines about penetrating or emerging through layered barriers. The expression occurs 824 times in 248 allowlisted files representing 246 independent works. Counts range from one to ten thousand barriers; one passes, breaks, opens, guards, or remains separated by them. Yuantong Daomin warns, ‘do not say no-mind is the Way; no-mind still leaves one further barrier.’ Dun'an Zongyan asks who in the assembly has passed it. An unnamed monk asks Daxiu Zhu to present ‘the final barrier,’ while another unnamed monk asks how to pass ‘this barrier’ and Xueguan Zhiyin directs him to ‘ask the gatekeeper.’ Baoshou Xin speaks of going straight through two barriers, and Wuzu Fayan speaks of passing four. A late discourse by the Yongzheng Emperor gives its own named description of ‘passing through the further barrier’; this is preserved as that text’s account, not made universal. Zen bends the checkpoint image into a public measure, but the corpus names no fixed numbered stage shared by every use.

Occurrences.Kwic: 非君子之所談汝豈不見華嚴經云剎說眾生說三世一時說洞山後到溈山山問承聞价闍黎曾問國師無情說法是不洞云是溈云試請舉看洞便舉溈云我這裏也有秪是罕遇其人
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (P/P154/P154n1519.xml). Essential Compendium of the Zen School. Guishan Lingyou asks Dongshan Liangjie whether he had questioned National Teacher Nanyang Huizhong; Guishan utters the title within that question.

Senses.Explanation: Ācārya is a title or direct form of address for a monastic instructor; in ordination compounds it can designate the office-holder who performs a defined ceremonial role. In encounters the title is often spoken directly to the person being questioned or answered. The bare title does not by itself decide rank, lineage, or ordination office.
